title: Minority cultures of the world
titleCn: 世界少数民族文化：多贡人、沃达贝人等

paragraphs.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-six.
Hi, Paula.
Hello, Steve.
Wasn't that lecture brilliant yesterday on the world's indigenous peoples?
What? Dr. Smith's introduction to the anthropology option?
Yes. It's quite worrying to think that so many minority cultures are endangered.
I know. My own problem is that I was so interested in what he was saying that I didn't take proper notes.
[chuckles] Don't you remember the main ideas, like that group in Mali, the Dogon people, knowing so much about astronomy?
Yes, I remember that. They know about the brightest star. That's Sirius, having a smaller, unseen companion star that circles it and pulls it off course.
And that the invisible companion star takes fifty years to go round its own orbit.
Amazing without telescopes. And of course, not in my notes.
Oh.
Look, Steve, have you got a minute to go over the main points with me?
Okay. L-let me see what I wrote. Next were the Wodaabe, who grazed their cattle across large areas of land in a West African country called Niger.
I remember that.
Now, I've got something here about the Wayewa in Indonesia.
Mm, Dr. Smith said they've got some fascinating traditions, like assessing a person's wealth by the number of people owing them a favor.
That's a really original banking system. I wonder if it would work here.

Then there were the Gabra people in northern Kenya, who are traditional camel herders. Dr. Smith commented on the way they manage the land, even land that's been overgrazed by other groups. They've become a model for semi-desert management, anticipating drought and preparing for it.
I remember him saying something about a group in Brazil, the Xavante people.
Oh, yeah.
There's a project to repopulate the forest with game and fruits in their home area, so they can go back there to the traditional lifestyle they've lost. They're actually increasing in numbers.
Yes, that's great.
Then there were the Makuna people. They had really interesting ideas.
Yes. They believe that man and the animal world are one, don't they?
Mm-hmm, and they have taboos against hunting and fishing in certain places so that stocks of animals and fish are maintained.
Here's the last name in my notes: the Navajo people in the USA. Of course, I'd heard of them before. Dr. Smith said they'd found minerals such as coal, oil, and uranium in their lands.
But when they tried to sell these sources of power, this led to a number of disputes.
Right.
Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-seven to thirty.
Now listen and answer questions twenty-seven to thirty.
I just completely gave up in the next part of the lecture.
When Dr. Smith tried to look at similarities between groups?
That's right. I got lost.
Well, you don't need to write everything down.
Yes, I know, but I just haven't got the hang of it yet.
You remember the Wodaabe headgear and cosmetics in the slides? Really elegant. They feel beauty is an essential quality in life.
And didn't he say the Navajo have the same idea?
Exactly. It's a major feature of their culture. Then Dr. Smith compared the Gabra and the Wayewa.
What, both being nomadic?

No, the Wayewa are actually settled, but both particularly value sharing. The Gabra give or loan animals so that others do the same for them in time of need. And then the Wayewa have a special ceremony when groups drag huge stones with ropes with loads of onlookers.
Must be spectacular.
I suppose it shows that people can achieve more that way.
Now, I do remember something about the Dogon and Wodaabe being similar.
Well, they're both from Western Africa, but that wasn't his main point.
What then? Drought?
No. Dr. Smith was talking in terms of their skills in music.
That's right. I heard some on air. Really impressive.
And then the Makuna and the Wayewa have similar problems because their governments both want to promote a particular model of education.
Which doesn't match their own ideas of what's important.
Correct.
I'll just make a note of that.
Okay, now, uh... So another pair in totally different areas of the world, the Xavante and Gabra-
From South America and Africa?
Yes. Both are under pressure to settle in specific locations.
That would be difficult for them.

Almost impossible if they're trying to preserve their traditions. And the last point of comparison was between the Makuna and Wayewa, because central to both their cultures is the giving of gifts. In the first case, from the natural world, which gives up its animals and fish to the world of man for food, and in the second, from man to his ancestors, who gave him life.
That's really brilliant, Steve. Now I can see the value of good notes to get the main points. Oh, it would really be a tragedy if all these cultures disappeared.
That is the end of part three. You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to Part three.
